explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. The speaker says, “I, the LORD, am its keeper…” No hired hand and no middle manager, just the LORD. A vineyard with that keeper is in good hands.

No king is mentioned in these verses, friend. The speaker says it Himself: “I, the LORD, am its keeper…” Even a king with a big crown would need a nap sometime, but the LORD waters it continually. So this keeper is not a person on a throne.
The priests don't show up in this part of the passage at all. The speaker says, “I, the LORD, am its keeper…” That settles who has the job. Nobody else gets handed the watering can.
Close, baker, but the text says more than daytime. The LORD says, “I guard it night and day…” So the guarding doesn't stop when the sun goes down. Think of a bakery that never turns off the lights.
Yes, it's false. The LORD says, “I guard it night and day…” That covers the whole clock, not just the daylight hours. No shift change, no coffee break.
That's the word, baker. The LORD says He guards it “so no one can disturb it.” The guarding has a purpose, and the text names it. Nobody gets to mess with that vineyard.
Nothing in the text says anyone is trying to sell the vineyard. The LORD says He guards it “so no one can disturb it.” So there's no for-sale sign anywhere in these verses. The word is disturb.
Good guess if you're picturing a hide and seek game, friend. But the text says the LORD guards it “so no one can disturb it.” Nobody is hunting for the vineyard here. The word is disturb.
Yes, baker. Right after the guarding, the LORD says, “I am not angry.” That comes in verse 4. A guard who isn't angry, that's worth noticing.
This one is true, friend. The text has the LORD say, “I am not angry.” It comes right after He talks about guarding the vineyard. So the answer sits right there in verse 4.

explanations.answer: Trample them and burn them down
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, “I would march and trample them, I would burn them to the ground.” He says it about thorns and briers if they confronted Him. Those are strong words, and the text says them plainly.

explanations.answer: Let them grow next to the vines
explanations.explanation: The text says the opposite, friend. The LORD says He would “march and trample them,” and He would “burn them to the ground.” So no sharing the garden bed. Thorns and vines don't get to be neighbors here.
Moving day never comes up, baker. The LORD says, “I would march and trample them, I would burn them to the ground.” He doesn't run from the thorns and briers. He faces them.
Right, baker. The LORD says, “let them make peace with Me…” Right after the thorns and briers, the door is open for peace. The text puts it right there in verse 5.
Nobody gets sent away in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “let them make peace with Me…” That's the other thing He says to let them do. Peace is the offer on the table.

No offering is mentioned here, baker. The LORD says to let them lay claim to His protection and to “let them make peace with Me…” That's all the text asks of them in this verse. No gift basket required.

explanations.answer: It takes root and fills the world with fruit
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The text says, “Jacob will take root. Israel will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit.” That's a big picture for the days to come. It starts with roots and ends with fruit all over the world.

explanations.answer: It stays small and hidden in one field
explanations.explanation: This plant doesn't stay in one field, friend. The text says Israel will “fill the whole world with fruit.” That's about as far from hidden as it gets. It grows big.

explanations.answer: It blooms once but never bears any fruit
explanations.explanation: Blooming is only part of it, baker. The text says Israel “will bud and blossom and fill the whole world with fruit.” So the fruit does come, and a lot of it. This plant finishes the job.
Yes, baker. The text says, “By warfare and exile You contended with her…” This is a heavy part of the passage. The LORD is the one who contended with Israel here.
This one is true, friend. The text says, “By warfare and exile You contended with her…” It's a heavy line. The words are plain, and they're right there in verse 8.
That's the word, baker. The text says, “Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for…” After all that hardship, this is where it turns. Guilt gets covered, and that's a good word to hear.
The text doesn't say land here, friend. It says, “Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for…” So it's the guilt that gets dealt with. The word is guilt.
Jacob's name isn't what gets atoned for, baker. The text says, “Jacob’s guilt will be atoned for…” The name is just who the verse is about. What gets atoned for is guilt.

explanations.answer: He makes all the altar stones like crushed chalk
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says “…makes all the altar stones like crushed bits of chalk…” That's the full fruit of the removal of his sin. And with it, no Asherah poles or incense altars will remain standing.

explanations.answer: He builds a taller altar of stone
explanations.explanation: The text goes the other direction, friend. Nothing gets built taller. “…all the altar stones like crushed bits of chalk…” is the picture. The stones get crushed, not stacked.

explanations.answer: He sets up new carved idols
explanations.explanation: New idols don't make it into this verse, baker. The text says no Asherah poles or incense altars will remain standing. The fruit of the removal of his sin is the altar stones crushed like chalk. It's about taking things down, not putting more up.

Yes, baker. The text says, “There the calves graze, and there they lie down…” The fortified city is deserted, so the calves have the place to themselves. The city looks very different from a stronghold now.
This one is true, friend. The text says, “There the calves graze, and there they lie down…” The city lies deserted. So the calves are the ones making themselves at home.

explanations.answer: They are a people without understanding
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says, baker. “…for this is a people without understanding.” Then it says their Maker has no compassion on them. The reason is given right there in verse 11.

explanations.answer: They live too far from Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Distance isn't the reason given, friend. The text says, “…for this is a people without understanding.” That's why their Maker has no compassion on them. Jerusalem's address has nothing to do with it here.

explanations.answer: They lost a long war to Egypt
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a war with Egypt here, baker. It gives one reason: “…for this is a people without understanding.” That's why their Maker has no compassion on them. Egypt shows up later in the passage for a different reason.
Exactly, baker. The text says, “…you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one.” Every single person counts. Nobody gets lumped into a crowd and lost.
Pairs sound neat, friend, like a buddy system. But the text says, “…you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one.” It's single file, not pairs. Each person is gathered on their own.
Sorting by tribe makes a tidy plan, baker. But the text says, “…you, O Israelites, will be gathered one by one.” No tribes are named in the gathering. It's person by person.
Right, baker. The text says, “…a great ram’s horn will sound…” That's the sound in that day. It comes right before those in Assyria and Egypt come forth.
Thunder would get everybody's attention, friend, but it's not in the verse. The text says, “…a great ram’s horn will sound…” So the sound is a horn. No storm clouds here.

A bell is close to my heart, baker, since Ruby, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like one. But no bell rings in this verse. The text says, “…a great ram’s horn will sound…” The sound is a horn, not a bell.
Not quite, baker. The text says, “…those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt.” Both groups come forth. Nobody is left behind in Egypt.
Yes, it's false. The text says, “…those who were perishing in Assyria will come forth with those who were exiles in Egypt.” They come forth together, from both places. Nobody stays behind.

explanations.answer: On the holy mountain in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: That's the place, baker. The text says, “…they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.” That's where the passage ends. Worship is where they're headed.

explanations.answer: At the altar in the city of Bethel
explanations.explanation: Bethel never comes up in this passage, friend. The text says, “…they will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.” So the place is Jerusalem. That's the last stop on this trip.

explanations.answer: In a temple in the land of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt is where some of them were exiles, baker. But the text says they “will worship the LORD on the holy mountain in Jerusalem.” They leave Egypt to do it. The worship happens in Jerusalem.
